lead: A fix is two or more position lines that cross: bearings, transits, ranges, depths. Each has its errors, the compass two of its own. Check one source against another.

sections.title: From the compass to the chart

qa.q: Do I apply deviation to a bearing taken with a hand-bearing compass?
qa.a: No, not if you use it in the open, clear of steel, engine and speakers: a **hand-bearing compass** then needs variation only. A bearing over the steering compass also takes the deviation for the ship's head.

refs: Variation — annual change and the nearest rose
Hand-bearing compass — deviation found on a transit

blocks.p: Bearings are plotted in true. A **hand-bearing compass** used in the open, clear of steel, engine and speakers, needs variation only: add east, subtract west. Take it from the nearest rose, updated to this year.

A bearing sighted over the **steering compass** also takes deviation: that of the ship's head, not of the bearing, interpolated in the card. The card serves that compass only; an error found for the hand compass on a transit holds at that spot and heading.

fig.title: Bearing over the steering compass
lines: Hand compass, clear of steel: only the −2°

sections.title: Find the deviation before you need it

qa.q: How do I check my compass deviation using a transit?
qa.a: Steer along a charted **transit**, convert its true bearing to magnetic and compare with the compass: reading high means deviation west, low means east. Offshore, use the tabled bearing of the rising or setting sun.

refs: Compass — checking deviation on a transit
Compass — checking on a transit astern

blocks.p: **Deviation** is the boat's own magnetism: engine, keel bolts, wiring. It changes with the heading and with heel. Anything magnetic left near the compass adds more: a phone, a steel tool, a kedge, a live cable. Aluminium does not.
Measure it by steering along a charted **transit**. With the marks astern you are on its reciprocal; offshore, use the tabled bearing of the rising or setting sun.

blocks.rule: Compass reads high: deviation west. Low: east.

blocks.p: The same error on every heading means a compass mounted out of line. **Swinging** repeats the check all round to make the card; redo it after fitting gear nearby. A **fluxgate** corrects itself after slow circles but needs power: the magnetic compass is the backup.

sections.title: Three bearings in the right order

qa.q: In what order should I take the bearings for a three-point fix?
qa.a: The marks ahead and astern first, as their bearings change slowly, and the mark abeam last, noting time and log with it. Choose marks about 60° apart; the three lines leave a **cocked hat**.

refs: Position fixing — a transit and a bearing

blocks.p: Choose marks that are fixed, sharp and charted exactly: a lighthouse, not a buoy or a sloping headland. Two lines cut best near 90°, three about 60° apart; marks ahead and astern give almost one line. A **transit** needs no compass: cross it with a bearing at right angles.

fig.note: Heading east: A and C first, B abeam last

blocks.p: Take the marks ahead and astern first, their bearings change slowly, and the mark abeam last; note time and log with that bearing. Three lines leave a **cocked hat**.

fig.note: Take the corner nearest the danger: C

blocks.p: A large cocked hat means a mistake: check each mark's identity and start again. A small one proves only that the bearings agree: if depth and EP both disagree, doubt it. A good fix beats the DR: restart from it, the gap being the stream left out. Fix as often as the danger demands: half a mile from rocks at 6 kn is five minutes.

sections.title: One mark, two bearings and the run between

qa.q: How do I get a fix from a single lighthouse with a running fix?
qa.a: Take two bearings of it, noting time and log, and transfer the first line along the **ground track** run between them, leeway and stream included. Where the transferred line cuts the second bearing is the fix.

refs: Running fix — course change and tide
Running fix — tide hour by hour
Running fix — bow and beam with tide
GPS failure — a running fix at night

blocks.p: With one mark, take a bearing and note time and log; later take another. From any point on the first line lay off the **ground track** run between them, leeway and stream included, and redraw the first line through its end. Where this transferred line cuts the second bearing is the fix.

fig.note: 45° on the bow, then abeam: distance off = the run

blocks.p: Whenever the angle on the bow doubles, distance off at the second bearing equals the run, over the ground if there is a stream. After an alteration, add the legs and the stream end to end. One mark's line can be crossed with another's bearing. Every error of course, log and stream goes into the fix: keep the run short and prefer two marks at once.

sections.title: Range from the horizon, name from the stopwatch

qa.q: How do I work out my distance off when a light rises over the horizon?
qa.a: It is 2.08 × (√H + √h) miles, H being the light's height and h your eye's, in metres: the range at which a strong light **rises**. Cross that range with the light's bearing for a fix.

refs: Position lines — rising and dipping lights
Position fixing — rising light and bearing
Rising and dipping lights — bobbing a light
Rising lights — height of tide on the light
Rising lights — identifying a landfall light
Fixing at night — identifying a light
Fixing at night — timing a light

blocks.p: On a clear night a strong light **rises** over the horizon at 2.08 × (√H + √h) miles, H being its height and h your eye's, in metres. Cross that range with its bearing for a fix.

list: If the nominal range is less, the light shows late, already above the horizon.
Charted heights are above MHWS: at a lower tide add the difference.
The loom is not the light, and haze spoils the method.
Bob your head: seen standing, gone sitting, and you are at that distance.

blocks.p: Name a light before using it: count the flashes and time the full period, from one group's start to the next. Occulting shows more light than dark. If two lights share a character, your EP and their ranges decide.

sections.title: Ranges and soundings as position lines

qa.q: How do I fix my position with radar?
qa.a: By **ranges**, not bearings: radar measures range well and bearing poorly. Cross two ranges, or a range with a visual bearing, with the VRM on the near edge of a steep target; where two arcs cross twice, the depth decides.

refs: Radar — range with a visual bearing
Radar — range of a low target
Fixing in fog — a line of soundings
Fixing in fog — radar and plotter

blocks.p: Radar measures **range** well and bearing poorly: fix by two ranges, or a range crossed with a visual bearing. Put the VRM on the near edge of a steep target; a low beach may not paint, leaving the hills behind as first echo. A low target shows only inside the radar horizon, 2.2 × (√h + √H). A head-up EBL reads from the bow: add the heading. Excess sea-clutter control hides small close echoes; rain control breaks up a shower.
The sounder gives a position line too, once the sounding is reduced to chart datum.

fig.note: 13.2 − 3.2 = 10.0 m below datum: you are at B

blocks.p: Two range arcs cross twice: the depth says which. In fog a line of soundings can be matched to the chart; a fog signal gives no bearing. When radar and sounder agree against the plotter, believe them and stand off.

sections.title: A position to check, not to obey

qa.q: How do I plot a GPS position quickly on a paper chart?
qa.a: As a **range and bearing** to a waypoint charted on a known object. The bearing runs from you to the waypoint, so you lie on its reciprocal; check whether the set shows true or magnetic.

refs: GPS — range and bearing to a waypoint

blocks.p: Plot a GPS position quickly as a **range and bearing** to a waypoint charted on a known object. The bearing runs from you to the waypoint, so you lie on its reciprocal; check whether the set shows true or magnetic.

fig.note: You are 3.2 M from the waypoint, on 220°T from it
